readerTitle: Why "tasty and clean" won't win you customers
caseNote: 가상 사례 (라멘 가게, 인보이스 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용 · 개념은 Keller 외(2002) 브랜드 포지셔닝 연구에 근거
insight: 고객이 '가장 중요하다'고 말하는 것과 고객이 '당신을 고르는 이유'는 다르다. 차별점은 중요도가 아니라 '중요하면서 당신만 하는 것'에서 나온다.
misconception: 고객이 가장 중요하다고 답한 항목(맛, 청결, 가격)을 앞세우면 선택받는다.

sources.text: Keller, K. L., Sternthal, B., & Tybout, A. (2002). Three Questions You Need to Ask About Your Brand. Harvard Business Review.
모든 설문 수치와 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 라멘 가게 설문 수치(92%/5%, 88%/3%, 80%/4%, 40%/85%, 10%/90%)는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 차트와 본문 숫자가 일치하는지 다시 확인하세요.
Keller·Sternthal·Tybout(2002) HBR 논문이 points of parity / points of difference를 다룬다는 점과 서지 정보(연도, 제목)를 게시 전 확인하세요. 카드에는 원문 인용 없이 개념만 요약했습니다.
인보이스 앱 사례의 '인터뷰 대상 프리랜서 대부분이 해외 고객 결제 지연을 겪음'은 가상 설정입니다. 실제 통계로 오해되지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 표시를 했습니다.

cards.title: Why "tasty and clean" won't win you customers
body: A ramen shop owner asks 200 customers what matters most. The top answers: tasty food, a clean room, fair prices.
So she puts those words on her window. Nothing changes. The survey wasn't wrong. She was reading the wrong column.

image.label: Ramen shop window with generic slogans
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 작은 라멘 가게 유리창에 "Tasty · Clean · Fair prices" 문구. 길 건너편 다른 식당 두 곳의 창에도 똑같은 문구가 붙어 있어 구분이 안 되는 장면. 실제 브랜드 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: What goes on the window?
body: The survey also asked a second question: *which of these can you only get here?* Your shop stays open until 2 a.m. and offers free noodle refills. No nearby shop does either.
You have room for one line on the window. Which do you choose?

options.text: "Tasty, clean, fair prices", the top-rated answers
options.feedback: Every word is true and important. But every rival can say it too, so it gives no one a reason to pick you over them.
It matters to a real group of customers, and they believe only you offer it. That combination is what moves choice. Next card shows the numbers.
Truly unique, which is good. But if few people care about it, being the only one doesn't bring many through the door.

cards.title: Two columns tell two different stories.
body: The top three items matter to almost everyone, yet almost no one thinks they're special to this shop. Late hours matter to fewer people, but 85% say only this shop offers them.

image.label: Matters-to-me vs only-this-shop
image.brief: Tasty/clean/price high importance low uniqueness; late hours reverse.

cards.title: Points of difference
body: A **point of difference** is something customers value, link to you, and believe they can't get as well anywhere else. It's the reason to choose you.
Its partner is the *point of parity*: things you must match just to be considered, like taste and cleanliness for a restaurant. Parity gets you on the list. Difference gets you picked.
Marketing scholars Kevin Lane Keller and colleagues made this split central to how brands position themselves.

cards.title: Three tests for a real difference.
body: A difference only works if it passes all three:
list: **Distinct:** they believe rivals don't offer it, or not as well
**Deliverable:** you can keep doing it, and customers believe you
cards.callout: Late hours pass all three. Free refills fail the first. "Tasty" fails the second.
cards.softwareNote: Feature comparison pages often list dozens of rows. Most are parity. The one or two rows only you can tick, and that buyers actually ask about, are your points of difference.

cards.title: Differences don't excuse weak basics, and they don't last forever.
body: Parity still counts. If the ramen is mediocre or the floor is sticky, late hours won't save the shop. Customers drop you before they ever weigh the difference.
Differences also get copied. If late hours start pulling customers, a rival can stay open too. Ask how hard your difference is to match, and keep looking for the next one.
Finally, check whose idea it is. A difference the owner is proud of but customers ignore is a hobby, not a position.

cards.title: Now it's an invoicing app.
body: Your app helps freelance photographers send invoices. In interviews, most say their biggest headache is overseas clients who pay late or in the wrong currency. Your app is the only one that sends invoices in the client's language and lets them pay in their own currency.

options.feedback: All three are must-haves, so leaving them out would hurt. But leading with them makes you sound like every other app.

options.text: "Get paid by overseas clients, in their language and currency"
options.feedback: It solves a pain users named, and no rival offers it. Keep the basics on the page, just not as the headline.

options.text: "The only invoicing app with 40 custom color themes"
options.feedback: Distinct, yes. But few photographers choose an invoicing tool for its colors, so the claim earns little.

cards.title: Match the basics. Win on what's valued and yours alone.
body: What customers say matters most is often what everyone already offers. Your reason to be chosen lives where *valued* and *only you* overlap.
**Try it today:** list five things customers like about your business. Mark each one: does a rival offer it too? The unmarked ones that customers care about are your points of difference.
